amendments.rule: **Hebrew has no verb *to have*, so an English *have* is a recasting and belongs to whatever made the clause possessive.** Where `הָיָה` is present it is the existential and takes the *have* itself, its preposition goes `unrepresented` under rule 40, and the suffix takes the subject pronoun: `וַיְהִי לוֹ נָשִׁים` → *he had* … *wives* puts *had* on `הָיָה` and *he* on the suffix. Where the clause is verbless, the possessive preposition is what makes it possessive and carries the *have*: `לָהֶם מִסְגְּרוֹת` → *they had panels* puts *had* on `לְ` and *they* on the suffix, and `שָׁפְרָה עָלָי` → *I have a goodly heritage* puts *have* on `עַל` and *I* on the suffix. Where neither is present, a possessive suffix can be the possession by itself and takes the supplied verb with its pronoun: `טוֹבָתִי בַּל עָלֶיךָ` → *I have no good beyond thee* gives the suffix *I have*, headed on the pronoun. Another finite verb in the clause does not qualify merely by being finite. `שָׁפְרָה` is not a copula: the ASV renders it by the attributive *goodly*, which is its lexeme, so the *have* is not its. **But a verb the ASV has itself rendered by the *have* does qualify, and the same subtraction decides it.** Where the Hebrew writes a verb of falling or allotment and the English writes *have* in its place — `יִפְּלוּ בְנַחֲלָה` → *they shall have inheritance* — dropping the word leaves that verb with no rendering at all, so the *have* is the verb's own together with the subject pronoun rule 17 keeps there, and a preposition beside it whose relation the ASV has left unstated goes `unrepresented` under rule 40. **And where nothing in the clause makes it possessive, the word is not to be placed at all.** A clause that writes no `הָיָה`, no possessive preposition, no suffix and no verb the *have* renders has no morpheme to carry it: `יוֹסֵף חֲבָלִים` → *Joseph* ***shall have two*** *portions* leaves the supplied verb its own `added` unit under rule 20's supplied-lexical-verb clause, together with any numeral, subject or object the ASV supplies alongside it, while the possessed noun keeps only its own word. Do not fold such a word into that noun, into a neighbouring clause's verb, or into a preposition standing elsewhere in the verse to avoid the `added`, for the reason rule 42 gives about a surplus *and*: it is written beside those renderings rather than inside one of them. Test by subtraction, as in rule 16 — drop the *have* and ask which morpheme has lost its rendering. If only the possession relation is gone, the *have* is the preposition's or the suffix's; if a written verb is left with nothing, it is that verb's; and if nothing in the clause is diminished but a possession the English has supplied, it is `added`. **Read *no possessive preposition* and *no suffix* in that count as none the ASV has left an English word for.** A preposition or a suffix on which the ASV has already spent its own word stands in the same position as an absent one: it is not what makes the clause possessive, and it is not a home for a second English word, exactly as rule 52 counts a preposition's function words against the morphemes that could carry them and rule 51 says a waw holding an English word of its own is not a home for a second one. What this rule's earlier sentences govern is a `בְּ` or a `לְ` that is itself the clause's predicate, for which the ASV writes no preposition at all — `אֲשֶׁר בּוֹ מוּם` → *that hath a blemish* — and not a locative or other phrase the ASV has rendered in full. `אוֹ תְבַלֻּל בְּעֵינוֹ` → *or* ***that hath*** *a blemish in his eye* writes *in* for the `בְּ`, *his* for the suffix, *eye* for the noun and *a blemish* for `תְּבַלֻּל`, so nothing is left for the *hath* to complete and it is its own `added` unit; `מְרוֹחַ אָשֶׁךְ` → ***hath his*** *stones broken* goes the same way, the adjective keeping *broken* and the noun *stones*, with the supplied *his* `added` besides under rule 18's closing sentence. Count the clause's English words against the morphemes that could carry them before reaching for one that is already spent. **And where the possessive clause is a relative clause, the written relative supplies the English subject and the resumptive suffix takes nothing.** `אֲשֶׁר בּוֹ מוּם` → *that hath a blemish* gives *that* to `אֲשֶׁר` and *hath* to the `בְּ`, and the suffix is `unrepresented` under rule 22, since two morphemes point at the antecedent and the ASV writes one word for it; the same clause written without a relative gives the suffix the subject pronoun this rule's earlier sentences direct, as `מוּם בּוֹ` → *he hath a blemish* does. A written `הָיָה` in such a clause still takes the *have* itself and leaves both the preposition and the suffix `unrepresented`: `אֲשֶׁר יִהְיֶה בּוֹ מוּם` → *that hath a blemish*.
amendments.why: Rule 43's `added` case enumerates its condition as a clause writing "no `hayah`, no possessive preposition, no suffix and no verb the *have* renders". LEV.21.20 met the substance of that condition while failing its letter: `'o tevallul be-'eyno` and `meroach 'ashekh` do write a preposition and a suffix, but the ASV has already spent *in* and *his* on them, so neither can carry the supplied *hath* without giving one morpheme two English words. Read literally the rule sends a verse pass hunting for a home and produces exactly the fold its own closing sentences forbid. The qualification is the contract's own counting reasoning — rule 52's "a preposition holding an English word of its own is not a home for a second one", rule 51's same sentence about a waw, rule 42's about a surplus *and* — applied to the morphemes rule 43 enumerates, so it narrows an over-broad sentence rather than adding new doctrine, and it contradicts nothing in the corpus tables supplied. The second addition qualifies the same rule's flat "the suffix takes the subject pronoun": LEV.21.17, 18, 19 and 21 write the possessive clause as a relative, where `'asher` is the English subject and the resumptive suffix has nothing left, against LEV.21.21 and 23 where no relative stands and the suffix does take *he*. Six instances in one chapter, cleanly conditioned on what is written, and the four unrepresented suffixes are the chapter's recurring BSB disagreement. Returned as an amendment rather than a new rule so the enumeration is corrected where a reader meets it.

conventions: Disqualification items: where a single participle or adjective is the whole of the item, the entire English clause the ASV builds around it joins that one morpheme's unit — pronoun, relative and supplied verb alike — under rules 46 and 31, as `charum` -> *he that hath a flat nose* and `sarua'` -> *anything superfluous* do at LEV.21.18, and `gibben` -> *crook backed*, `daq` -> *a dwarf* at LEV.21.20. Where the item instead writes further morphemes that each hold their own English, a verb the ASV supplies beside them is `added`: LEV.21.20's *hath* is added twice, before *a blemish in his eye* and before *his stones broken*, because `be-` holds *in*, the suffix *his*, `'ayin` *eye*, `tevallul` *a blemish*, `meroach` *broken* and `'ashekh` *stones*.

`'ish` heading a disqualification or eligibility clause takes the whole universalizing frame the ASV writes for it: *Whosoever he be* at LEV.21.17, where no `kol` stands, headed on *Whosoever*; *man he be* at LEV.21.18, where `kol` takes *whatsoever*, headed on *man*. The supplied *he be* is not given to a following preposition as a prepositional predicate's copula under rule 49, and is not `added`.

`'ishshey YHWH` -> *the offerings of Jehovah made by fire* is divided the same way at LEV.21.6 and LEV.21.21: `'ishsheh` takes *the offerings ... made by fire* as one discontinuous unit headed on *offerings* by rule 31's tie-breaker, the supplied *the* joining the construct under rule 29, while `YHWH` takes *of Jehovah*. *made by fire* is not split off and no morpheme of the phrase is left unrepresented.

`ki 'im` is one fused unit under rules 30 and 35 wherever it stands in this chapter — *except* at LEV.21.2, *but* at LEV.21.14 — and, neither morpheme carrying a lexeme, the source head is `ki`, the first token, as the deterministic display anchor.

report: Checked the chapter's one recurring construction end to end: the disqualification formula with a possessive `be-` + suffix. LEV.21.3, 17 and 19 write `hayah` and give it the have/copula, leaving the preposition and suffix unrepresented (rules 40, 43); LEV.21.18, 21 (twice) and 23 are verbless and give the have to the preposition. The suffix goes unrepresented in the four clauses where a written `'asher` supplies the English subject (17, 18, 19, 21a) and takes *he* in the two where none stands (21b, 23). That is one analysis conditioned on what the source writes, not two analyses; no patch.

Checked the supplied-English cases the lemma table is blind to. The chapter's only three `added` units are in LEV.21.20 (two *hath*, one *his*). They are not a split against LEV.21.18's *he that hath a flat nose*: there the whole English clause renders the single participle `charum` and no other morpheme stands in the item, while in LEV.21.20 every written morpheme of `tevallul be-'eyno` and `meroach 'ashekh` already holds its own English, so the supplied verb completes nothing. Rule 43's subtraction test gives that line; the verse notes name the competing reading.

Checked `'ish` (7 occurrences, 5 treatments in the table). LEV.21.17 *Whosoever he be* and LEV.21.18 *man he be* both fold the ASV's universalizing frame into `'ish`, the universal itself going to `kol` where one is written (21.18 *whatsoever*, 21.21 fused with `lo'` as *no* under rule 35) and to `'ish` where none is (21.17). Consistent.

Checked `'ishsheh` (LEV.21.6, 21.21): both take *the offerings ... made by fire* as one discontinuous unit headed on *offerings*. Checked the waw/`lo'` fusions (21.5 twice, 7, 10, 11, 12 twice, 23): all `aligned`, headed on the negative, with LEV.21.11's second *nor* correctly resting on a present `lo'` with a gapped waw. Checked the article count (rules 29, 41, 47) verse by verse: LEV.21.3's unrepresented `ha-` is right, the ASV writing *a virgin*.

One intra-verse choice left standing rather than patched: LEV.21.22 divides the superlative `qodshey ha-qodashim` as *holy* on the construct and *most* on the rectum, so the same `ha-qodashim` reads *most* in the first phrase and *holy* in the second. The reverse division is equally defensible and the unit's note already names it under rule 8; the accepted reading keeps the rectum's *the most* contiguous and maps head to head. Not a cross-verse split, so no edge was moved.

BSB disagreements: none is a genuine error. The 4 `R` cases are the le'mor lamedh (rule 27) and the possessive/recast prepositions of LEV.21.3, 17 and 19 (rules 40, 43); the 4 `Sp3ms` cases are the resumptive suffixes under a written `'asher` (rule 22); the LEV.21.3 article is rule 29. All four groups are the documented convention difference, BSB attaching each morpheme to its host phrase. No accepted edge was changed to improve the aggregate.

The one thing this chapter taught that the contract did not already say is that rule 43's enumerated condition — *no possessive preposition, no suffix* — must read a preposition or suffix the ASV has already spent a word on as absent. Returned as an amendment to rule 43 rather than a new rule, so the over-broad enumeration is corrected where a reader meets it.
